newsitem.title: INDIA: India scooter giant seen good despite sluggish sales.
newsitem.headline: India scooter giant seen good despite sluggish sales.

text.p: India's biggest maker of two-wheelers, Bajaj Auto Ltd, will ride out sluggish sales and little prospect of an early upturn to emerge stronger, analysts said on Wednesday.
"There'll be very slow growth this year," said S.M. Athalye, associate vice president (investments) at Tata Asset Management Ltd. "The sluggish pick-up in demand is a matter of concern."
But the company is the best bet in the industry and will continue to outperform other firms, he said.
James Capel B&K auto analyst Anupam Thareja believes the scooter giant will beat the temporary slowdown and emerge stronger than others.
"It is the lowest cost producer with almost double the margin of its competitors," he said.

Indian scooter sales during November 1996, the latest month for which official figures are available, dropped to 59,663 scooters from 63,489 a year ago, according to the Association of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (AIAM).

Sales of motorcycles in November were higher at 25,734 against 21,383 in the same month of 1995. But sales of mopeds -- lightweight mini-powered scooters -- fell to 5,541 from 8,225 in November 1995. Sales of three-wheelers shrank to 13,068 units from 13,426, the AIAM figures showed.
The scooter giant's problems were a reflection of the slowdown in the industry, analysts said.

"What is particularly worrying was that the overall industry sales were lower in the three segments of scooters, mopeds and three-wheelers and Bajaj Auto was no exception," said auto analyst Manish Gupta at Khandwala Finances Ltd.
He said the slack demand was the result of tight money conditions and an overall economic slowdown.
"People have deferred purchases," he said. "The middle class have begun to feel the pinch."

Gupta saw little prospect of an upturn in the near future. Further, the company is unlikely to match the substantial "other income" it got by deploying surplus funds in liquid financial instruments, he said.

"The company had an other income of almost 1.09 billion rupees in the first half," Gupta said. "This is likely to be lower in the second half due to lowering of interest rates... and locking-up of part of surplus funds for inventory."

He revised his sales forecast to 35.88 billion rupees for the financial year ending March 31, 1997 from his earlier estimated 33.38 billion. The revised profit after tax was 4.55 billion rupees against previously projected 5.06 billion.
For 1995/96 (April-March) the company reported a net profit of 4.18 billion rupees and net sales of 27.94 billion.
In the first six months 1996/97, it made a net profit of 2.26 billion rupees against 1.77 billion in the year-ago period. Net sales were 16.03 billion rupees against 12.81 billion.
Gupta said profit growth for the whole year would be about 8-10 percent against the 27 percent rise in the first half.
